soil-meth-029.title: Gas chromatography, sorting compounds as vapor
soil-meth-029.text: Some chemicals can be turned into vapor without breaking apart, and that is all gas chromatography needs. It is a way of separating a mixture, here made of compounds that vaporize without decomposing, and then analysing each part. Among the {{ref:soil-chem-078}}, it measures chemicals in soil, air or water, including the gases held in soil. It also works inside other instruments. The Dumas nitrogen method, described in {{ref:soil-meth-021}}, ends with a gas chromatography column that pulls nitrogen apart from carbon dioxide and water.

soil-meth-021.title: Burning soil to learn what it is made of
soil-meth-021.text: One quick way to learn what a soil contains is to set it on fire. Elemental analysis measures the elemental, and sometimes isotopic, composition of a material such as soil. Its commonest form, CHNS analysis, for carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and sulfur, works by combustion: the sample burns and the oxidized products are measured. CHN analyzers borrow the flash combustion of the Dumas method. A sample burns at 800–900 °C in oxygen, {{ref:soil-meth-029}} separates the released nitrogen, and a thermal conductivity or infrared detector reads it. Each Dumas measurement takes a few minutes and uses no toxic chemicals or catalysts. The older {{ref:soil-meth-020}} takes an hour or more.

soil-meth-024.title: Reading a soil's elements in the glow of a plasma
soil-meth-024.text: Inside the instrument burns a plasma of argon at 6000 to 10,000 K. Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy, shortened to ICP-AES or ICP-OES, uses that heat to excite atoms and ions until they emit light. Each element shines at its own wavelengths, and the intensity there is proportional to its concentration. A pump feeds the sample to a nebulizer, which sprays it as a mist directly into the plasma. Detector arrays read all the wavelengths at once, so every element the unit can sense is analysed together, and quickly. Comparing line intensities with calibration curves of known standards gives the concentrations. The method has largely replaced older ones such as gravimetric analysis for routine trace work on many elements. It is fast becoming the method of choice for nutrient levels in farm soils. In a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}, those levels set the fertilizer a crop needs for yield and quality. Its skill with trace elements even helps forensic scientists trace the origin of soil found at crime scenes.

soil-meth-023.title: Atomic absorption: metals caught by the light they absorb
soil-meth-023.text: Each metal absorbs light only at its own wavelengths. Atomic absorption spectroscopy uses this to measure the concentration of metals in a sample. The metals are vaporized in a flame, and the radiation each absorbs is proportional to the density of its atoms. Alan Walsh's team at CSIRO in Melbourne developed the modern form in the 1950s, and it now serves fields from agriculture to medicine. Soil extracts from batch equilibration are commonly analysed this way. The flame version works in the mg/L range; the graphite-furnace version is 2–3 orders of magnitude more sensitive.

soil-meth-019.title: Loss on ignition: weighing what the furnace takes away
soil-meth-019.text: A furnace and a balance are all this test needs. In a loss-on-ignition test, a soil or mineral sample is heated strongly at a set temperature until its mass stops changing. The weight lost measures the volatile components driven off. A few grams go into a crucible weighed empty and already fired. They are weighed, heated in a temperature-controlled furnace for a set time, cooled in a dry, CO2-free atmosphere and weighed again. Left overnight in a drying oven at 100 °C, a sample loses all its water, which gives its dry weight and so its original water content. The test typically estimates water, carbon, {{ref:soil-found-045}} and volatile compounds. Samples burned down a profile show the organic content at each depth. A sudden rise down the profile, with other clues, is strong evidence of a buried soil surface invisible to the eye. Weighing continuously as the temperature changes is a variant called thermogravimetry.

soil-meth-020.title: The Kjeldahl method: nitrogen from a flask of boiling acid
soil-meth-020.text: Measuring nitrogen the slow way starts with a flask of hot acid. The Kjeldahl method is a wet-chemistry test, done with liquid reagents, that measures the organic nitrogen plus the ammonia and ammonium in a sample. The sample is digested in concentrated sulfuric acid at 360–410 °C. The acid oxidizes the organic matter and holds the reduced nitrogen as ammonium sulfate. Catalysts such as selenium, Hg2SO4 or CuSO4 speed the digestion, and Na2SO4 or K2SO4 raises the acid's boiling point. Sodium hydroxide then turns the ammonium into ammonia gas, which is distilled into a standard acid and measured by titration. The result, total Kjeldahl nitrogen or TKN, is reported in analyses of soil, water and waste water. Besides foods, the method assays soils, waste waters and fertilizers. Without modification it misses other inorganic nitrogen such as nitrate. Its hot concentrated acid and an hour or more per test compare poorly with the faster Dumas method in {{ref:soil-meth-021}}.

soil-meth-025.title: ICP-MS, counting ions down to parts per quadrillion
soil-meth-025.text: Its range starts at 1 part per quadrillion and runs up to 100 ppm. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, or ICP-MS, ionizes a sample in the same kind of plasma as {{ref:soil-meth-024}}, then counts the resulting ions. That lets it detect metals and some non-metals at very low concentrations. It covers atomic masses 7 to 250, lithium to uranium, and tells isotopes apart. It is faster, more precise and more sensitive than {{ref:soil-meth-023}}, and it scans all elements at once. Its uses run from water testing to soil analysis. Measuring Fe2+ and Fe3+ in ancient rocks even reveals the redox potential of ancient soils.

soil-meth-026.title: Ion chromatography, sorting ions by their grip
soil-meth-026.text: This separation method traces back to clay. Thompson and Way treated clays with fertilizer salts and found ammonia retained and calcium released, the swap now called {{ref:soil-chem-047}}. Ion chromatography turns that swap into a tool. It separates ions and ionizable molecules by their affinity for an ion exchanger. Anion-exchange columns carry a positive stationary phase, the fixed material inside, that holds negative ions. Cation-exchange columns carry a negative one that holds positive ions. It is a popular method for anions and complexes in environmental problems, and one of the methods used to analyse soil extracts.

soil-meth-018.title: Fine earth: the part of soil 2 mm and smaller
soil-meth-018.text: Soil scientists draw a line at 2 mm. The particles that size or smaller make up the fine earth fraction; coarser pieces such as {{ref:soil-phys-044}} fall outside it. In the {{ref:soil-class-016}}, the whole soil is the fine earth plus coarse fragments, artefacts, cemented parts and dead plant residues of any size. Many of its horizon criteria are percentages by volume related to the fine earth, such as the share of rock structure in an A or B horizon. On granite in cool climates, feldspars weather slowly and sand comes to dominate it. Its makeup also shapes {{ref:soil-found-051}}: a loam can lose its desirable qualities when clay is dispersed throughout its fine earth.

soil-meth-027.title: Ion-selective electrodes turn one ion into a voltage
soil-meth-027.text: A thin membrane can turn chemistry into electricity. An ion-selective electrode is a membrane sensor that converts the activity of one specific ion in solution into an electrical potential. The pH glass electrode is a very common type. The voltage is read against a reference electrode, and it depends on the logarithm of the ion's activity, following the Nernst equation. These electrodes are among the methods used to analyse soil extracts, and they serve environmental science and agriculture. They have one weakness. Readings drift with temperature and time, so they need frequent recalibration against standards, ideally before and after each sample.

soil-meth-022.title: Ammonium acetate, the cation that evicts the others
soil-meth-022.text: To count the cations a soil holds, chemists first push them off. Ammonium acetate extraction does that job. The ammonium ion acts as a replacement cation, taking over exchange sites and displacing potassium and the other bound cations. The extract serves to measure {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and available potassium. Ammonium is one of the cations used most often for this in {{ref:soil-chem-051}}. The chemistry hides a catch. A pure ammonium acetate solution has a pH of about 7, yet it buffers only around pH 4.75 and 9.25, not at pH 7.

soil-meth-028.title: Phosphorus turns blue: the molybdenum test
soil-meth-028.text: Phosphate can be made to turn a solution blue, and the depth of blue tells how much is there. In the molybdenum blue test, phosphate is mixed with an acid molybdate solution, and the complex is reduced to its blue form, for example by ascorbic acid. The color's depth is proportional to the phosphorus concentration. However phosphorus leaves the soil for solution, it is usually detected this way. Labs use a colorimeter; field workers use detector sticks and a color chart. Comparable amounts of arsenate spoil the test, since arsenate behaves much like phosphate. Mapped on archaeological plans, soil phosphate shows former activity areas and helps prospect for sites.

soil-meth-030.title: The soil thin section, a slice thin enough for light
soil-meth-030.text: Ground down to about 30 μm, a slice of soil lets light straight through. A soil thin section is such a slice of rock, mineral or soil, mounted on glass for study under a polarizing microscope. Soil micromorphology describes far more in it than a 10x hand lens can show. Between crossed polarizing filters, the optical properties of minerals alter the color and intensity of the light, so most rock-forming minerals can be identified. Quartz usually serves as the gauge of thickness, checked against the Michel-Lévy interference color chart. Thin sections reveal how a material's components relate to one another, features often invisible in a hand specimen. Micromorphologists have used them to characterize humus-form horizons. They also help identify paleosols: at least 60% recognizable pyroclastic fragments marks an Andisol paleosol.

soil-meth-031.title: Soil biofabric, the pellets left by ants and worms
soil-meth-031.text: Ants, worms and termites leave their signature in the soil's fabric. Soil biofabric is fabric made by organisms, typically small, often pelleted micro- and mesobiofabric, visible with a hand lens or in a {{ref:soil-meth-030}}. It is the mark of {{ref:soil-bio-047}}. As originally defined, a {{ref:soil-form-055}} must show at least 50% biofabric. Burrowing vertebrates and uprooted trees make something coarser: megabiofabric, cloddy surface spoil heaps for which the 50% criterion is moot.

soil-meth-032.title: Minerals that turn cloudy as they weather
soil-meth-032.text: Under the microscope, weathering shows itself in each grain. Mineral alteration is the change natural processes make to a mineral's chemical composition or crystal structure, as seen in a {{ref:soil-meth-030}}. Some minerals, such as feldspar, decompose readily and turn turbid. Quartz stays fresh and clear. Others yield characteristic secondary products. Thermodynamics governs the alteration under the prevailing conditions, and water is its most common and influential catalyst.

soil-meth-008.title: Geomorphometry, measuring the shape of the land
soil-meth-008.text: Water flows downhill, so the shape of the land can predict where streams will run. Geomorphometry is the science of measuring the shape of the land surface and the effects of that shape on human and natural processes. It works from digital elevation models, grids of ground heights, and extracts parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms. The most basic are slope, how steep the surface is, and aspect, the direction the slope faces. Slope is computed by discrete derivatives; the Horn method uses a cell and its eight neighbors. Thanks largely to the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and lidar, elevation models now cover almost all of Earth at 100 m resolution or better. The ideas go back to Brisson in 1808 and Gauss in 1827. The field grew mainly with GIS, geographic information systems, and elevation data sets from the 1970s. Its parameters improve the mapping and modeling of soils, serving {{ref:soil-agri-089}}, precision agriculture and soil-landscape modeling.

soil-meth-014.title: Ground-penetrating radar, echoes from buried layers
soil-meth-014.text: Radar can see into the ground, but how far depends on the soil. Ground-penetrating radar sends radio waves, usually between 10 MHz and 2.6 GHz, and records their reflections from buried boundaries, such as the edge of a {{ref:soil-found-001}}. Reflections occur where materials of different permittivity, an electrical property, meet. In dry sandy soils it reaches up to 15 m; in moist or clay-rich soils, only a few centimeters. Clay soils and salt-contaminated soils limit it most, and rocky soils scatter the signal. Higher frequencies trade penetration for resolution. It is used to study soils and bedrock, and cross-borehole radar assesses the presence and amount of soil water.

soil-meth-015.title: Electrical resistivity tomography, imaging soil with current
soil-meth-015.text: A line of four electrodes can look underground. In electrical resistivity tomography, current passes between the two outer electrodes and voltage is read between the inner two. A geometric factor converts the result to apparent resistivity. As {{ref:soil-phys-042}} showed, wetter soil is less resistive, and dry and saturated soil can differ by orders of magnitude. Clays conduct through their charged particle surfaces as well as their pore water. Electrode spacings of 0.75 to 12.0 m serve shallow surveys under 10 m, and depth is usually less than the widest spacing. It maps soil moisture for precision agriculture, images root zones and tracks contaminants in soil and groundwater.

soil-meth-011.title: Multispectral imaging: a few bands beyond sight
soil-meth-011.text: A single image can show water depth, vegetation cover and soil moisture at once. Multispectral imaging captures data in a small number of separate wavelength bands, typically 3 to 15, including bands beyond visible light. Mid-infrared bands at 1550–1750 nm image vegetation and soil moisture. Far-infrared bands at 2080–2350 nm image soil, silicates and clays. Surface and subsurface soil differ spectrally. Disturbed soil emits more at 8.5 to 9.5 micrometers, which helps detect buried land mines. {{ref:soil-meth-012}} goes further, often with hundreds of contiguous bands.

soil-meth-012.title: Hyperspectral imaging, a full spectrum in every pixel
soil-meth-012.text: Every material leaves a characteristic spectral signature, and that signature can identify it. Where {{ref:soil-meth-011}} records a handful of bands, hyperspectral imaging records a full, finely resolved spectrum across many continuous bands for each pixel. Sensors on aircraft, satellites or drones use it to investigate plants and soils remotely, assessing ground cover and soil chemistry. In farming it is being used to detect the nutrient and water status of wheat and heavy-metal stress in plants. It is often treated as a surface technique, yet it can probe beneath the surface, to a depth set by the spectral range and the sample.

soil-meth-010.title: NDVI: reading plant health in red and near-infrared light
soil-meth-010.text: Healthy leaves absorb visible light and throw back near-infrared. Chlorophyll strongly absorbs light from 400 to 700 nm, while leaf cell structure strongly reflects near-infrared from 700 to 1100 nm. The normalized difference vegetation index, or NDVI, turns that contrast in red and near-infrared bands of {{ref:soil-meth-011}} into a measure of vegetation health and density. Values run from -1 to 1. Near zero means little or no vegetation, negative means water, and high means dense healthy vegetation. Bare soils give about 0.1 to 0.2. Because wet soil darkens, a change in soil moisture can shift the index with no change in vegetation. The soil-adjusted and enhanced vegetation indices correct for such soil background effects.

soil-meth-005.title: Why no two spots in a field are alike
soil-meth-005.text: A field known down to the last grain would still vary from spot to spot. Spatial variability is the way a quantity measured at different places takes different values from place to place. It is not the same as uncertainty. Uncertainty depends on how the field was sampled as well as on how much it varies. Spatial descriptive statistics such as the range can describe variability. Those descriptions carry uncertainty of their own, since interpolation methods differ. {{ref:soil-meth-001}} has been used to study how the sorption and degradation of a {{ref:soil-env-237}} vary across a field. Precision agriculture studies variability within fields, such as how terrain and soil properties affect crop growth and water distribution. Urban landscapes and golf courses show high variability in soil composition, unlike uniform farm fields.

soil-meth-001.title: Geostatistics, from ore mines to farm fields
soil-meth-001.text: This branch of statistics began underground, as a way to predict the distribution of ore grades in mines. Geostatistics deals with spatial or spatio-temporal data, and it now serves soil science and agriculture, especially precision farming. Simpler interpolators such as {{ref:soil-meth-007}} came first. Geostatistics goes further by treating values at unsampled places as correlated random variables. A model of spatial continuity, often a parametric form of the {{ref:soil-meth-002}}, describes how strongly nearby values constrain the value at an unsampled point. Using one model across a whole area assumes stationarity, the same statistical properties everywhere; several methods relax that assumption. The work serves two goals. One is estimating the most likely value at each place. The other is simulating many alternative maps, called realizations, that together give probabilistic forecasts. Bayesian inference plays a growing part, implementing {{ref:soil-meth-003}} through a Gaussian process updated with Bayes' theorem.

soil-meth-002.title: The variogram: how difference grows with distance
soil-meth-002.text: Soil samples taken far apart vary more than samples taken close together. The variogram puts a number on that pattern, and it is the key tool of {{ref:soil-meth-001}}. It is a graph or function of how much pairs of observations differ according to the distance separating them. Matheron defined the semivariogram in 1963 as half the average squared difference between values a distance h apart, such as the iron content of soil. Since nobody can sample everywhere, an empirical variogram is built from the squared differences between every pair of sample points. It is not guaranteed to be valid, so a model is fitted to it, most often linear, spherical, Gaussian or exponential. Three features summarize it. The nugget is a jump at the origin, and the sill is its limit at large distances. The range is where it nears the sill, often taken as 95% of it. The fitted model sets the weights used in {{ref:soil-meth-003}}. Usage is muddled: some authors call the semivariogram a variogram, and the word semivariance can mislead.

soil-meth-006.title: Filling the gaps between sample points
soil-meth-006.text: No survey can measure every point, so the gaps are filled by estimate. Spatial interpolation estimates the values of a quantity at arbitrary places from values known at a set of points. Geostatistics uses it to build digital elevation models from spot heights or survey depths. For scattered points the methods include nearest-neighbor and natural-neighbor schemes, {{ref:soil-meth-007}}, variants of {{ref:soil-meth-003}}, and thin-plate or other splines. Gridding converts irregularly spaced data into a regular grid. GIS software produces interpolated surfaces with methods like these, and with trend surfaces.

soil-meth-003.title: Kriging, the best guess between boreholes
soil-meth-003.text: It started with a few boreholes in South Africa's Witwatersrand. Danie Krige's thesis estimated gold grades from them, and Georges Matheron built on it to set out the theory of kriging in 1960. Kriging predicts a value at an unsampled point as a weighted average of nearby known values, based on a model of their covariance. The weights come from the fitted {{ref:soil-meth-002}}. Under suitable assumptions it gives the best linear unbiased prediction, or BLUP. Ordinary kriging picks weights that minimize the mean squared error, and they sum to 1 so the estimate is unbiased. Its estimation variance grows as samples lie farther from the target point. That variance depends on the sampling layout, not on the sample values. Only one realization of the random function is ever observed, so kriging must assume some degree of stationarity. Variants include simple, ordinary, universal and indicator kriging, and co-kriging of related variables. The basic form is computationally heavy, but approximations scale it to larger problems.

soil-meth-004.title: Regression-kriging: letting terrain and satellites guide the map
soil-meth-004.text: Part of a soil property's pattern follows the landscape, and part behaves like chance. Regression-kriging models the two separately, as Matheron's 1969 {{ref:soil-agri-093}} proposed. It first regresses the target variable on auxiliary layers, such as terrain from {{ref:soil-meth-008}} and remote-sensing images, fitting the trend by ordinary or generalized least squares. The leftover residuals are interpolated by {{ref:soil-meth-003}} and added back. The method is mathematically equivalent to universal kriging and kriging with external drift. With no spatial autocorrelation it reduces to multiple regression; with no useful covariates, to ordinary kriging. Odeh and colleagues named it in 1995, and Minasny and McBratney call it the empirical BLUP. It maps soil properties wherever covariate layers correlate significantly with the property. Those layers keep multiplying, from near-global topography at about 90 m from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission to MODIS images at 250 m. Yet Minasny and McBratney found that more, better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.

soil-meth-007.title: Inverse distance weighting, a freshman's fix
soil-meth-007.text: In 1968 Donald Shepard, a Harvard freshman, was overhauling the interpolation in the SYMAP mapping program. The method he published, inverse distance weighting, estimates an unknown value as a weighted average of known points, each weighted by the inverse of its distance. Nearer points count for more, and no random model is involved. Shepard tested exponents of distance and settled near -2, close to the gravity model. It was among the simpler interpolators known before geostatistics. In Slovenia's Idrija area, it was used in GIS to turn soil samples into a raster map of mercury concentration.

soil-meth-009.title: The topographic wetness index: where hillslopes stay wet
soil-meth-009.text: Where a hillside gets soggy can be read from two quantities. The topographic wetness index combines the upslope area draining through a point, per unit contour length, with the local slope in radians, a basic product of {{ref:soil-meth-008}}. This steady-state index quantifies how topography controls hydrological processes. Areas with similar values become saturated under similar moisture conditions. Beven and Kirkby developed it within the TOPMODEL runoff model. It correlates highly with soil attributes such as horizon depth, silt percentage, organic matter content and phosphorus. It was designed for a hillslope {{ref:soil-form-054}}, and it is not meaningful on flat ground.

soil-meth-017.title: SoilGrids, a soil map of the whole world
soil-meth-017.text: The world's soil properties are now mapped in cells of 250 m. ISRIC produces those maps with SoilGrids, a system for automated global soil mapping. Machine learning fits models to the WoSIS database of soil profiles and to more than 400 global environmental covariates, and the maps come with quantified uncertainty. Like {{ref:soil-meth-004}}, it predicts soil properties from environmental layers. SoilGrids and the WoSIS database are ISRIC's flagship soil information products.

soil-meth-016.title: Mapping the soils of the Moon and Mars from orbit
soil-meth-016.text: Cosmic rays make the soils of the Moon and Mars shine in gamma rays. The rays strike nuclei in the soil, releasing neutrons and exciting nuclei that then emit gamma rays of characteristic energy. Orbiting gamma-ray spectrometers read those emissions. The energy of each line identifies an element, and its intensity gives the concentration; about 20 elements can be measured. Neutron detectors sense hydrogen in the upper meter, revealing water ice. Mars Odyssey carried one with two neutron detectors. The method fails for bodies with thick atmospheres, such as Earth and Venus.

soil-meth-013.title: Near-infrared spectroscopy, a quick scan for soil tests
soil-meth-013.text: Near-infrared light travels deep into a sample before it is absorbed. Near-infrared spectroscopy uses the part of the spectrum from 780 nm to 2500 nm, where absorption comes from weak overtone and combination vibrations. Because the light penetrates far, bulk material can be probed with little preparation. The bands are broad and overlap, so readings need multivariate calibration, such as principal components or partial least squares, built on carefully chosen calibration samples. Karl Norris at the USDA pioneered it for agricultural products in the 1980s. It is valued as accurate, rapid, non-destructive and inexpensive, and soil-testing laboratories may use near-infrared scanning in a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

openers.meth: A soil sample that reaches the laboratory can be heated, burned, sprayed into a plasma and colored until it gives up its composition. Strong heating at a set temperature drives off volatile components, and the weight lost measures them. In an argon plasma, atoms and ions emit light that identifies each element, while a related instrument counts the ions themselves to catch metals at very low concentrations. Simpler tests work by color and voltage: phosphate forms a blue complex whose depth tracks its concentration, and a membrane sensor turns the activity of one ion into an electrical potential. This part begins with those laboratory methods.
openers.soil-analysis-and-laboratory-methods: Most soil analysis works on the part of a soil made of particles 2 mm across or smaller. Some tests first pull something out of it: an ammonium acetate solution displaces exchangeable cations, for measuring cation-exchange capacity and available potassium. Others separate what has been extracted, sorting ions by their affinity for an ion exchanger or vaporized compounds as gases. Then come the measurements, from wet chemistry that tracks organic nitrogen and ammonium to instruments that read the light atoms absorb or emit.
openers.soil-micromorphology: Many soil features are too small to see with the unaided eye. Soil micromorphology describes, measures and interprets them. Its central tool is a slice of soil ground to about 30 μm and mounted on glass for a polarizing microscope. In such slices the pelleted fabric left by ants, worms and termites shows up, along with the changes natural processes make to a mineral's composition and crystal structure.
openers.pedometrics-and-digital-soil-mapping: A quantity measured across a field takes different values from place to place, and a soil map has to capture that. Radar pulses and electrodes image what lies below the surface. Images taken in a few wavelength bands, or in many continuous ones, read soil and vegetation from above. A branch of statistics built for spatial data then describes how much pairs of observations differ with the distance between them. From that, unsampled points are predicted as weighted averages of their neighbors, and terrain and remote-sensing layers can sharpen the predictions further.

reviews.soil-analysis-and-laboratory-methods: The chapter's methods form a chain from sample to number. Laboratories work on the fine earth, displace exchangeable cations with ammonium acetate, and separate extracts by ion chromatography. Nitrogen comes from the Kjeldahl method's hot acid in an hour or more, or from Dumas combustion and gas chromatography in a few minutes. Metals are read from the light their atoms absorb or emit, or counted as ions by ICP-MS down to 1 part per quadrillion. Simpler tools still earn their place: a furnace and balance give organic content down a profile, a blue color gives phosphorus, and an electrode gives one ion's voltage.
reviews.soil-micromorphology: Under the microscope, a soil becomes a record of its own history. A thin section shows how its components relate to one another, features often invisible in a hand specimen. Ants, worms and termites leave pelleted biofabric, and a biomantle as originally defined must be at least 50% biofabric. The minerals record weathering, as feldspar turns turbid while quartz stays fresh and clear. Together these clues help identify paleosols, such as an Andisol paleosol marked by at least 60% recognizable pyroclastic fragments.
reviews.pedometrics-and-digital-soil-mapping: Mapping soil starts from a plain observation: samples far apart differ more than samples close together. The variogram measures that change, and kriging uses it to weight nearby samples when predicting unsampled points. Regression-kriging adds covariates, from terrain derived by geomorphometry to satellite images, while SoilGrids fits machine learning models to profiles and over 400 covariates to map the whole world. Ground-penetrating radar and resistivity image what lies beneath, and multispectral and hyperspectral sensors read the surface from above. Even so, more and better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.
